analysis.one_liner: Consolidates federal food safety into a new agency with mandatory inspections, recalls, and import standards.
analysis.headline: The food safety overhaul drew 41 cosponsors but never received a committee markup or floor vote, dying when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have pulled all federal food safety work out of the FDA and other agencies into a new Food Safety Administration with a single director. It required food companies to prevent contamination rather than react after outbreaks, created minimum inspection schedules, allowed the government to order recalls, required imported food to meet the same standards as American food, and added whistleblower protections. It never got a vote in either committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats: fewer foodborne illnesses through mandatory prevention controls, faster outbreak tracing through a national traceability system, government-ordered recalls of contaminated food, equal standards for imported food, and whistleblower protection for industry employees who report contamination. Consumers with weakened immune systems, infants, and the elderly — the groups the bill's findings single out as most at risk — would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Food Safety Administration in HHS headed by a Senate-confirmed Administrator with full-time responsibility and budget authority for food safety, fixing the fragmentation the bill's findings describe at the FDA.

Shifts the legal framework from reacting to outbreaks after they happen toward preventing them: all food establishments must adopt preventive process controls, sanitation plans, and performance standards for the most dangerous contaminants.

Establishes a national inspection program with regular, unannounced visits and minimum frequencies by risk category — continuous inspection for slaughterhouses, weekly for the riskiest processors, at least annual for warehouses and transporters.

Gives the government real enforcement power: authority to suspend a facility's registration after a hearing, detain or seize food, and order recalls, plus civil and criminal penalties and a presumption favoring the agency in adulteration cases.

Requires all imported food to meet standards at least equal to U.S. food, with a certification system for foreign governments and accredited third-party auditors, audits of foreign facilities, and penalties for countries that refuse U.S. inspections.

Builds a national traceability system so contaminated food can be traced through every stage of production and distribution during a recall, and strengthens foodborne illness surveillance with CDC, including DNA fingerprinting of pathogens.
Protects food industry employees who report safety violations from retaliation, and allows citizen civil actions against violators.

analysis.who_pays: Food companies bear most of the cost: slaughterhouses, processors, warehouses, and transporters must register annually, adopt preventive controls, keep extensive records, submit to inspections, and face fines, registration suspension, and forced recalls for violations. Farms and ranches — defined as food production facilities — must adopt written safety plans and standards for fertilizer, water, and hygiene, and open records to inspectors. Importers and foreign suppliers pay certification and inspection fees. Taxpayers fund the new agency, its inspectors, and grants to state and local health departments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food processors, farms, importers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill reaches onto the farm: it defines a food production facility as any farm, ranch, orchard, vineyard, or aquaculture operation, and requires written food safety plans, science-based standards covering fertilizer use, water, and animal encroachment, and open access to farm records. Small and organic growers argued this burden threatened family farms, and the bill offers technical assistance and a variance process but no blanket exemption for small producers.

The inspection mandates are rigid floors, not flexible targets — continuous inspection on every slaughter line, weekly random visits for riskiest processors — which would require a large, sustained increase in federal appropriations; the bill authorizes funding but caps the authorization in Section 508, leaving a gap Congress would have to fill every year.

The restructuring is disruptive: the bill strips food safety functions from the FDA (renaming it the Federal Drug and Device Administration) and from NOAA's seafood inspection program, and moves personnel and assets into a new agency, with transition risk and cost during the reorganization.
Compliance costs would be passed through to grocery prices, and heavier paperwork falls hardest on small businesses even with the bill's technical assistance provision.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and broad — a prevention-based system with real recall authority addresses a risk every household shares — while the costs fall on identifiable industries and partly on taxpayers. The honest concerns are design ones: the on-farm mandates were drawn broadly enough to alarm small growers, the fixed inspection frequencies commit Congress to significant annual spending, and the agency reorganization carries transition risk. The bill's small-business assistance, variance process, and whistleblower protections partially address the fairness concerns, but a good-faith critic could argue a narrower bill targeting the highest-risk facilities would capture most of the benefit at less cost — which is roughly the direction Congress eventually went in other legislation.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to two committees, which sent it to their subcommittees, and it sat there with no markup, no vote, and no further action until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on February 4, 2009, with 30 original cosponsors, citing findings that the FDA's food safety program was 'not effective in controlling hazards' and that the governing law was 70 years old and largely reactive.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to two committees — Energy and Commerce and Agriculture — splitting jurisdiction between the agencies and farms the bill would regulate.
On February 9, 2009, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; on April 23, 2009, to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry.
Neither subcommittee nor full committee ever held a markup or vote, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the 111th Congress.
The bill attracted 41 cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican signed on and no floor vote ever occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large food processors, importers, and farms avoided the bill's registration, preventive-control, inspection, and recall mandates, and the FDA kept its existing structure and food safety duties. Consumers did not get the stronger prevention-and-recall system this bill proposed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, but the bill's support was entirely Democratic: all 41 cosponsors were House Democrats and none of the chamber's 178 Republicans signed on.

industries.note: The bill imposes annual registration, mandatory preventive process controls, performance standards for the worst contaminants, minimum inspection frequencies, extensive recordkeeping, and penalties including forced recalls and registration suspension. Its interest in avoiding those compliance costs runs against the public's interest in safer food.

Defined as 'food production facilities,' farms would face written safety plans, science-based standards for fertilizer, water, hygiene, and animal encroachment, and open access to their records. Small growers' resistance to on-farm regulation collided with public demands for safer produce after repeated outbreaks.

Imported food would have to meet U.S. standards, pass through accredited certification, enter at designated ports, and submit to audits — with import denial for non-cooperating countries. Importers had profited from the weaker monitoring the bill's findings describe.

Seafood inspection moves from NOAA's Fisheries Service to the new Food Safety Administration, and seafood plants face ongoing verification and at least weekly random inspections. Standards continue but under a new, more assertive regulator.
The bill creates a program accrediting laboratories to perform required sampling and testing, with annual on-site audits — a new stream of accredited work for qualified labs.
